title: Index is address plus i.
lede: An array is one block. Slot i lives at base + i × size — O(1), no hop. Append at the end is O(1) if capacity remains. Insert or delete in the middle shifts the tail — O(n). Binary search, two pointers, prefix sums all assume this layout.
diagram: Left (hit): Array [7|2|9|4] indices 0..3. a[2] → address+2×4 = 9. Right: rotate-right-by-k example k=2: reverse all, reverse [0,k), reverse [k,n). 1 2 3 4 5 → 4 5 1 2 3. Caption: in-place, O(1) extra space.
what: Fixed-size or dynamic contiguous slots of one type. Get/set O(1). Scan O(n). Cache-friendly because the next index is the next cache line. 2D: row-major a[r][c] is a[r*cols+c].
why: Default structure in screens. Rotate array, move zeroes, Dutch flag, prefix sums — they mutate the block. Say index, length, in-place vs extra array.
trap: a[n] is out of bounds — the last index is n-1. 'Insert is O(1)' — only at the end with spare capacity. Treating a Python list as a linked list: it is a dynamic array (plate 102).

title: Capacity doubles. Append is cheap.
lede: A vector is an array plus a length and a capacity. Push when length < capacity writes one slot. When it is full, allocate 2×, copy, then write. One push is O(n) on resize; n pushes are still O(n) total — amortized O(1) each. pop from the end is O(1) and usually does not shrink.
diagram: Three steps: 1 len=3 cap=4 [a b c _] push d → [a b c d] O(1). 2 full, push e → alloc 8, copy 4, write e. O(n) this call. 3 geometric series: 1+2+4+…+n = 2n-1 copies. Average < 2 copies per push.
what: length = live items. capacity = allocated slots. Geometric growth (×2 or ×1.5) is the trick that makes append amortized O(1). Insert at i still O(n) — you shift, even with spare cap.
why: Language 'arrays' (Java ArrayList, Python list, C++ vector, JS Array) are this. Interviews: 'why not grow by +1?' Because n resizes of size 1,2,3,… cost O(n²).
trap: Amortized is not worst-case: a single push can stall on a copy of n. Real-time code uses a ring (plate 105) or a pre-sized array. Also: mid-insert is still O(n) after a resize.

title: A dummy node saves the empty case.
lede: Each node holds a value and next. You do not have index i. You have a pointer. Reverse, merge, unlink: three pointers and a dummy head so you never special-case 'the list was empty' or 'we replaced head'.
diagram: Left (hit): dummy → 1 → 2 → 3. Insert/delete after dummy; return dummy.next. Right: reverse. prev=null, cur=head; while cur: nxt=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=nxt. Walk 1→2→3 becoming 3→2→1. Caption: O(n) time, O(1) space.
what: Singly: one pointer forward. Head is the only entry. Tail append is O(n) unless you store tail. Dummy (sentinel) is a fake node before head — one code path.
why: SDE-1: reverse list, merge two sorted, remove nth from end (two pointers + dummy), palindrome list. Draw the boxes. Then write the three lines.
trap: cur = cur.next after you already set cur.next = prev — you lost the rest. Save nxt first. Also: dummy.next is the real head; returning dummy is a bug. Recursing n=10^5 blows the stack — iterate.

title: Prev makes splice O(1).
lede: A doubly-linked node has prev and next. If you already hold the node, unlink is four pointer writes — O(1), no scan. LRU cache is a hashmap from key to node plus this list for recency. The map finds; the list splices.
diagram: Nodes: dummyH ⇄ A ⇄ B ⇄ C ⇄ dummyT. Unlink B: A.next=C, C.prev=A. Move B to tail (most recent): unlink, then attach before dummyT. O(1). Caption: always keep two dummy sentinels so head/tail are never null.
what: Four links to cut a node (its neighbors and its own prev/next). O(1) only if you have the node. Finding by value is still O(n) — that's why LRU pairs it with a hash map (plate 150).
why: LRU, LFU's recency list, browser history, deque internals. Interview design: 'O(1) get and put' forces hash + DLL. Say both.
trap: Forgetting to update both directions — a one-way splice corrupts the list. Deleting while iterating without saving next. Using a singly list for LRU and scanning for the victim — that's O(n), not O(1).

title: Head and tail walk a circle.
lede: A ring is a fixed array plus two indices. Push writes at tail, then tail = (tail+1) % cap. Pop reads at head, then head = (head+1) % cap. Full and empty must be distinguishable — store a count, or keep one slot empty.
diagram: Left (hit): cap=4, [7|2|_|_] head=0 tail=2 count=2. push 9 → tail=3. pop → 7, head=1. Right: wrap. head=3 tail=1 [9|4|_|8] — logical order 8,9,4. Caption: no alloc on push. Overflow is a policy: reject, or overwrite the oldest.
what: Bounded queue in O(1) time and O(1) extra memory after the array exists. Producer/consumer, sliding window of last k, audio buffers. Modulo wraps the indices.
why: Interviews: implement a circular queue (LeetCode 622). Name head, tail, count (or the empty-slot rule). Bounded work queues in services are this.
trap: head==tail meaning both empty and full — you cannot tell. Keep count, or a boolean, or waste one slot (full when (tail+1)%cap==head). Also: % on negative indices in some languages.

title: The last in is the first out.
lede: A stack is LIFO: push and pop the same end. Recursion is a stack the CPU already has (plate 56). Interviews: match brackets, decode a string, monotonic next-greater (plate 153). Draw the growing column. The top is the only live choice.
diagram: Left (hit): valid parentheses. s='([])'. stack empty → push ( → push [ → pop ] matches [ → pop ) matches (. empty at end = valid. Right: mismatch. '(]' — pop expects ), got ]. Also leftover opens at end. Caption: map )]} to partners. Only push opens.
what: Array-backed stack: push/pop O(1) amortized. Linked stack: O(1) true. Peek is top without pop. Empty is the base case.
why: DFS, undo, parse, 'next greater' (monotonic). SDE-1 greatest hit: Valid Parentheses. Min Stack is plate 151. Nested structure → stack.
trap: Popping empty. Comparing types wrong: '(' vs ')'. Using a queue. Sorting the string — order of nesting is the whole point. Recursing n=10^5 instead of an explicit stack.

title: The first in is the first out.
lede: A queue is FIFO: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front. BFS is 'the people who arrived first get processed first' — that is why a queue gives unweighted shortest path and tree level order. A list pop(0) is O(n); use a deque.
diagram: Tree 1 / \ 2 3 / 4. Queue snapshots: [1] → pop 1 push 2,3 → [2,3] → pop 2 push 4 → [3,4] → pop 3 → [4] → pop 4. Levels: [1] | [2,3] | [4]. Caption: record q.length at the start of a level if you need level order.
what: Enqueue O(1), dequeue O(1) with a ring or deque. Peek front. BFS visits closer nodes first. Tree level order is BFS on a tree.
why: Islands, word ladder, course-schedule Kahn, binary-tree level order. If the interviewer says 'shortest in an unweighted graph,' you said queue before you said code.
trap: Using a Python list with pop(0) — O(n) per pop, O(n²) BFS. Recursing 'BFS' — that's DFS. Not capturing level size so a zigzag/level problem becomes a flat visit.

title: Both ends are doors.
lede: A deque (double-ended queue) pushes and pops at both ends in O(1). Sliding-window maximum keeps candidates in a deque of indices, front = max (plate 136). Palindrome check: pop both ends. Implement a queue with a ring, or two stacks — different trade.
diagram: Three boxes: Stack = one door (LIFO). Queue = in back, out front. Deque = both. Worked: window k=3 on [1,3,-1,-3,5] deque holds decreasing values. Front is the max of the window.
what: O(1) push/pop front and back. Random access is not promised (a ring deque can index; a linked deque cannot cheaply). Python collections.deque, Java ArrayDeque.
why: Sliding window max/min, 0-1 BFS (push front if weight 0), palindrome, undo/redo with two ends. When both ends move, it is a deque not a stack.
trap: Java Stack class (synchronized, extends Vector) vs ArrayDeque. Indexing a linked deque as if it were an array. Using deque as a list and scanning the middle — O(n).

title: Need a pair? Store the complement.
lede: A hash map is key → value in average O(1). The two-sum pattern: walking i, look up target − a[i]; if present you have the pair; else store a[i] → i. One pass. The map remembers what the left side already saw.
diagram: Left (hit): a=[2,7,11,15] t=9. i=0 store 2→0. i=1 need 2, found 0 → [0,1]. Right: group anagrams. key = sorted letters or 26-count tuple → list of words. Caption: plate 51 is the machine; this plate is the move.
what: get/put/delete average O(1). Iterate items O(n). Keys need hash + equals. Value can be an index, a count, a list of positions.
why: Two-sum, subarray sum equals k (prefix + map, plate 126), group anagrams, clone graph (old node → new). First tool when the naive pair loop is n².
trap: Unsorted two-sum with two pointers (plate 54) — that needs sorted data and loses indices. Storing the current index before looking up — a number that is twice itself false-hits. Mutable keys.

title: Have I seen this?
lede: A hash set is a map with no values — only membership. Add, remove, contains: average O(1). The interview line is 'seen'. First duplicate, longest consecutive sequence (start a run only if n-1 is missing), a sliding window of unique chars.
diagram: 1 Walk [3,1,4,1]: seen {3,1,4}, 1 already in → first dup. 2 Longest consecutive: put all in set; for x, if x-1 not in set, count x, x+1, …  O(n) because each number is a start at most once. 3 Window: set of chars in [l,r]; repeat → shrink l.
what: Membership. No order (HashSet). Need order? TreeSet / ordered set (plate 125) is log n. Python set, JS Set, Java HashSet.
why: Dedup, 'exists', graph visited, union of two arrays. Consecutive sequence is the trick that looks sort-O(n log n) and is O(n) with a set.
trap: Checking 'x-1 in set' inside the count loop without the start-of-run test — becomes O(n²). Using a list as 'seen' — contains is O(n). Floating keys and NaN. Assuming iteration order.

title: Two children. That's the tree.
lede: A binary tree node is value, left, right. No other promise: it is not sorted (that's a BST, plate 112), not complete (that's a heap, plate 114). Height is longest root-to-leaf. n nodes: height from log n (balanced) to n (a stick).
diagram: Left: node diagram. 4 / \ 2 7 / \ 1 3. Not a heap, is a BST. Right: same values as a stick 1-2-3-4-7. Height 4 vs 2. Caption: null children are the base of recursion. Array form: i → 2i+1, 2i+2 only if you store the holes.
what: Recursive structure. Size = 1+size(L)+size(R). Height = 1+max(hL,hR). Traversals on plate 57. Level order uses a queue (plate 107).
why: Invert, diameter, path sum, LCA, serialize — all 'recurse both kids, combine.' Draw one node and two boxes before you code.
trap: Calling a random binary tree a BST. Using 2i+1 indexing on a sparse tree without placeholders — you skip holes wrong. Returning height 0 for a single node vs 1 — pick a definition and stick to it (empty = -1 or 0).

title: Left is less. Right is more.
lede: A BST orders keys: whole left subtree < node < whole right. Search, insert: walk one child, O(height). Inorder walk emits sorted keys (plate 57). Unbalanced, height is n and you have a slow sorted list.
diagram: Left (hit): tree 6 / \ 3 8 / \ 1 5. Search 5: 6→3→5. Search 7: 6→8→null. Right: delete 3. Successor (min of right) or predecessor. Two children is the hard case. Caption: validate BST is plate 169 — bounds, not 'left < node < right' on one node only.
what: Average O(log n) if random or balanced. Worst O(n) on sorted inserts. Successor of x = leftmost of right, or the last ancestor you turned left from.
why: Search, floor/ceil, kth smallest (inorder count), validate, LCA in a BST (walk until split). Ordered map internals (plate 125).
trap: Inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST — it becomes a list. Checking only immediate children for 'is BST'. Duplicate policy: usually left or disallow; say it.

title: Height must stay log n.
lede: A balanced BST rewrites the tree on insert/delete so height stays Θ(log n). AVL: each node keeps |hL − hR| ≤ 1, then rotates. Red-black: color invariants, same big-O, fewer rotations. TreeMap / std::map are this, not a hashmap.
diagram: Insert 1,2,3 without balance: a stick, height 3. AVL insert 3 into 1-2: left-left? It's right-right on 1. Rotate left at 1 → 2 / \ 1 3. Balance factors -1,0,1. Caption: four cases LL, LR, RR, RL. LR is left rotate child then right rotate node.
what: Search/insert/delete O(log n) worst-case. Rotation is local pointer surgery that preserves inorder (so it stays a BST) and restores height.
why: Why TreeMap beats a HashMap when you need ordered keys, range, floor/ceiling. Why a hashmap is still faster for pure lookup. Interviews: 'how does a balanced tree stay log n?' Rotations.
trap: Calling HashMap balanced. Implementing AVL in a screen — they usually want the idea and a rotation diagram, not 80 lines. Also: heap is balanced-as-complete, but not a search tree (plate 58, 114).

title: Parent is at (i-1)/2.
lede: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array. Index i has parent (i−1)//2, kids 2i+1 and 2i+2. Sift up after push, sift down after pop. Min-heap: parent ≤ kids. You cannot find an arbitrary key in O(log n) — that is a BST.
diagram: Left (hit): array [1,3,2,7,4,5] drawn as tree. 1 / \ 3 2 / \ / 7 4 5. Parent of index 4 (value 4) is (4-1)/2=1 (value 3). Right: push 0. append, sift up swapping with parent until heap order. Caption: pop = swap [0] with last, pop, sift down.
what: Push O(log n), pop min/max O(log n), peek O(1), build O(n) bottom-up. Complete = filled level by level, so the array has no holes.
why: Priority queue (plate 115), top-k, Dijkstra, heap-sort. Interviews: 'implement a heap' means this indexing plus sift.
trap: 1-based vs 0-based formulas mixed. Using a heap as a search tree. Assuming heapsort is stable. Python heapq is a min-heap — max-heap via negatives.

title: Always pop the next best.
lede: A priority queue pops the smallest (or largest) currently stored, not the oldest. Under the hood: a heap. Keep k, don't sort n (plate 63). Dijkstra pops the closest unsettled node. Merge k lists pops the smallest head (plate 161).
diagram: Three boxes: 1 Top-k frequent — min-heap of size k on counts. 2 Dijkstra — heap of (dist, node). 3 Scheduling — next task by deadline. Caption: peek is O(1), push/pop O(log n). Change-priority is not always offered (binary heap is O(n) find); Dijkstra often pushes duplicates.
what: Abstract: insert + extract-min. Concrete: binary heap. Fib heap is theory. If you need decrease-key often, say so.
why: Any 'next best' loop. Meeting rooms II (min heap of end times, plate 159). Median stream uses two (plate 164).
trap: Sorting every insert — O(n) insert. Using PQ for FIFO (that's a queue). Forgetting Java PriorityQueue is a min-heap; max needs a comparator or negatives.

title: Name the neighbors.
lede: An adjacency list stores, for each node, the edges out of it. Sparse graph: n nodes, m edges, memory Θ(n+m). Walk neighbors of u in degree(u) time. This is the default. A matrix (plate 117) wins only when the graph is dense or you need O(1) 'is uv an edge?'
diagram: Left (hit): nodes 0..4. edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4. list: 0:[1,2] 1:[0,3] 2:[0,3] 3:[1,2,4] 4:[3]. Right: directed 0→1→2, 0→2. 0:[1,2] 1:[2] 2:[]. Caption: BFS/DFS/Dijkstra iterate g[u]. Weighted: store (v,w) pairs.
what: Undirected: add both ways. Directed: one way. Weights on the pair. Isolated nodes still need an empty list so n is known.
why: Course schedule, islands-as-graph, clone graph, word ladder (implicit list: other words). Interview: build the list first, then BFS.
trap: Forgetting the reverse edge on undirected. Using a matrix on n=10^5, m=10^5 — memory dies. Iterating all n to find neighbors of u.

title: An edge is a cell.
lede: A matrix g[n][n] has g[u][v] = 1 (or weight) if the edge exists. Query is O(1). Memory is Θ(n²) whether the graph is empty or full. Walking neighbors of u scans a whole row — O(n), even if degree is 2.
diagram: Left: same 5-node path-ish graph as 116, 5×5 grid of 0/1, symmetric for undirected. Diagonal 0 (no loops). Right: dense complete K4 — list would store 12 directed pairs, matrix is 16 cells and neighbor scan is the same O(n) anyway. Caption: Floyd-Warshall wants a matrix. BFS on a sparse graph does not.
what: O(1) edge test, O(n) neighbor scan, Θ(n²) space. Weighted: store the weight, use ∞ for missing. Directed: not symmetric.
why: n is tiny (≤400), or the algorithm is DP on i,j (Floyd, transitive closure). Some problems give the matrix already (image grid is different — plate 118).
trap: n=10^4 matrix. Assuming undirected symmetry on a directed graph. g[u][u]=1 meaning a self-loop vs a visited mark — don't reuse the matrix as a visited array without a plan.

title: A grid is a graph of cells.
lede: A 2D grid is a graph you do not store. Each cell (r,c) has up to four neighbors. BFS/DFS with a visited matrix (or mutating the cell) is the whole algorithm for islands, flood fill, shortest path in a maze. Flatten index i = r*cols+c when you need a 1D visited set.
diagram: 1 Cell (r,c) → (r±1,c), (r,c±1). Bounds check first. 2 Number of islands: for each 1, DFS mark 0, count++. 3 Shortest in binary maze: BFS queue of (r,c,dist), 4-dir, skip 0s. Caption: 8-dir is the same plus diagonals — only if the problem says so.
what: n = rows*cols nodes, m ≤ 4n edges. Time O(n). Space O(n) visited / queue. Don't build an explicit adj list.
why: Number of islands, rotting oranges (multi-source BFS), surrounded regions, unique paths with obstacles, word search. If it is a matrix of cells, think grid-graph before '2D DP'.
trap: Recursing DFS on a 1000×1000 grid — stack overflow; iterate or BFS. Forgetting bounds. Using 8-dir when the spec is 4. Mutating the input without saying you will.

title: Find the root. Merge the smaller.
lede: Union-Find (Disjoint Set) tracks components. find(x) walks parent pointers to a root. union(a,b) hangs one root under the other. Path compression (point to root on the way up) plus union by rank/size makes almost O(1) per op — inverse Ackermann, in practice a tiny constant.
diagram: 1 parent = [0,1,2,3,4] each alone. 2 union(0,1) union(1,2) — tree 2←1←0 or flattened 0,1,2 → root 2. 3 find(0)==find(2) yes. union(3,4). 4 components = number of roots. Caption: redundant connection: union returns false if already same root.
what: Dynamic connectivity. Kruskal MST. Accounts merge, number of provinces, graph valid tree. Array parent[n], rank[n].
why: When the graph is a stream of undirected edges and you only need 'same component?' — don't BFS every time. Offline queries too.
trap: Union without find — hanging a node under a non-root. Forgetting path compression so a stick becomes O(n). 1-based vs 0-based nodes. Directed graphs — DSU is for undirected membership.

title: Each node is a range.
lede: A segment tree is a binary tree over the array's ranges. The root is [0,n). Left is the first half, right the second. A node stores an aggregate (sum, min, gcd) of its range. Query and point update walk O(log n) nodes. Build is O(n).
diagram: Left (hit): a=[1,3,5,7] sum tree. Root 16 over [0,4). Kids 4 [0,2) and 12 [2,4). Leaves 1,3,5,7. Query [1,3) = 3+5 by mixing a full node and a leaf. Right: update index 2 to 10. Walk to leaf, set, walk up recomputing parents. Caption: tree array size ~ 4n.
what: Associative merge (sum, min, max, gcd). Point update + range query, or lazy range update. Index tree form or recursive with mid.
why: Range-sum / range-min with updates (Fenwick does prefix sums simpler — plate 121). Interview bar: say the invariant 'node = merge(left,right)' and O(log n).
trap: Building n². Off-by-one on half-open [l,r). Using a segment tree when a prefix array would do (no updates). Lazy propagation without a spec for range add — skip unless asked.

title: The index holds a prefix of bits.
lede: A Fenwick tree (BIT) is a prefix-sum machine in an array of size n+1. Index i is responsible for a range whose length is the last set bit of i. add(i,δ): while i≤n, t[i]+=δ, i += i & −i. prefix(i): while i>0, s+=t[i], i -= i & −i. Both O(log n).
diagram: 1-based. i=6 = 110b, last bit 2, covers two cells. i=8=1000b covers eight. Range sum [l,r] = prefix(r)−prefix(l−1). Update index 3 by +2 walks 3,4,8. Caption: i & −i isolates the lowest set bit (two's complement). Never use 0 as an index.
what: Point add + prefix query, or (via difference) range add + point query. Less general than a segment tree: inversion of the op should exist (sum yes, min no).
why: Count inversions (map values, add 1 as you scan). Frequency of ranks. Interview: 'range sum with updates' — Fenwick if it is prefix-shaped, segment if min/gcd.
trap: 0-based loops that never move (i+=i&-i on 0 is 0). Using Fenwick for range minimum. Off-by-one: prefix(r)−prefix(l−1), not prefix(r)−prefix(l).

title: If it never updates, precompute.
lede: A sparse table answers range min/max/gcd in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocess, if the array never changes. st[k][i] = f of 2^k elements starting at i. Overlap is OK because min (and gcd) do not care. Sum is not idempotent — overlapping would double-count, so sums stay prefix/Fenwick.
diagram: Left (hit): a=[2,4,1,6,3]. st[0]=a. st[1][i]=min(a[i],a[i+1]). Query [1,4]: k=floor log2(3)=1, min(st[1][1], st[1][4-2]) = min(min(4,1), min(6,3)). Right: why not sum — two overlapping blocks add the middle twice. Caption: k = 31-clz(len) or a precomputed log table.
what: Idempotent range ops: min, max, gcd, AND, OR. O(n log n) space and build, O(1) query. No updates.
why: Static RMQ, LCA in a tree after Euler tour. When the interviewer says 'array is immutable, many min queries.'
trap: Using it for sum. Updating one cell and forgetting the table is stale. Computing log inside a hot loop without a table is still fine; off-by-one on the second block index is the usual bug: j - (1<<k).

title: Maybe. Never a false no.
lede: A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions. Insert: set those k bits. Query: if any bit is 0, the item is definitely absent. If all are 1, it might be present — or those bits were set by others. False positives. No false negatives. You cannot delete (without counting).
diagram: Left (hit): 16 bits, k=3. Insert 'ada' sets 2,7,11. Query 'ada' all 1 → maybe. Query 'kai' bit 4 is 0 → no. Right: after many inserts, density high, everything looks like a maybe. Caption: pick m bits and k ≈ (m/n) ln 2 for a target false-positive rate.
what: Probabilistic set membership. O(k) time, tiny memory. No original keys stored. Cannot list items. Counting Bloom / Cuckoo for variants.
why: Caches ('is this URL even in the SSD set?'), DB to skip disk, spell-check, network. System + DSA crossover. Contrast a hash set: exact, stores keys.
trap: Treating maybe as yes. Deleting by clearing bits — you wipe other keys. Hashing poorly (k bits from one hash split badly). Using Bloom where a miss must be exact (auth, money).

title: Express lanes over a list.
lede: A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra forward pointers at coarser levels. Search starts on the top lane, drops when the next hop would pass the key. Expected height log n if each node joins the next level with p=1/2. Redis zset uses this.
diagram: Level 2: 1 ----------- 9. Level 1: 1 ---- 5 ---- 9. Level 0: 1-3-5-7-9. Search 7: 1→9 too far, drop; 1→5, 5→9 too far, drop; 5→7. Caption: insert finds the spot, coin-flips height, splices at each level. Expected O(log n) search/insert/delete.
what: Probabilistic alternative to a balanced BST. Simpler to picture than rotations. Ordered, range scan along level 0.
why: Interview: 'how does Redis sorted set work?' Skip list + hash. Also: why a list can still be log n if you add lanes.
trap: Deterministic 'every 2nd node' rebuild is a different structure (perfect skip) and painful to update. Worst case all height 1 if the coin hates you — expected, not worst-case like AVL. Not a replacement for a hashmap (no O(1)).

title: Keys stay sorted.
lede: An ordered map keeps keys in sorted order. Lookup is O(log n), not O(1). You gain predecessor, successor, range. Java TreeMap, C++ map, Python SortedDict — usually a balanced BST (plate 113) or a skip list (plate 124). A HashMap has none of the order ops.
diagram: Three boxes: HashMap — O(1) get, no order. TreeMap — floor(x), ceiling(x), first, last, submap. Example: timestamps of a key (plate 198) — binary search on a sorted list of ts is the same idea. Caption: iterate keys in order without a separate sort.
what: floor = greatest key ≤ x. ceiling = least key ≥ x. Insert/erase/get O(log n). Range iterate O(log n + k).
why: Leaderboards, time-based KV, 'next interval', sliding-window medians with two trees, exam room / number of flowers at t. When the problem says nearest key, not exact key.
trap: Using TreeMap for two-sum — log n for no reason. Assuming Python dict is ordered by key (it is insertion-ordered, not sorted). Mutating a key that participates in compare.

title: A range is two prefix lookups.
lede: prefix[i] = a[0]+…+a[i]. Sum of [l,r] = prefix[r] − prefix[l−1] (or prefix[r+1]−prefix[l] with a leading 0). Build O(n), each query O(1). Subarray sum equals k: walking r, look up how many prefixes equal prefix[r]−k — a hashmap of prefix counts.
diagram: Left (hit): a=[2,3,1,4] prefix=[0,2,5,6,10]. sum[1,3]=10-2=8. Right: subarray sum k=4. prefixes 0,2,5,6,10. At 6, need 2 — seen. [1,2] and [3,3] both 4. Caption: 2D prefix: S[r][c] includes the rectangle (0,0)→(r,c); inclusion-exclusion four corners.
what: Precompute running totals. Immutable array. Updates need Fenwick/segment (plates 120–121). Same idea for XOR (prefix xor, cancel twice).
why: Range sum, range average, pivot index, subarray sum k, number of subarrays with sum k, 2D region sum. If they ask many range sums and no updates, this not a nested loop.
trap: Off-by-one on the leading 0. prefix[r]−prefix[l] forgetting whether l is inclusive. Hashmap must count prefixes, not store one index, when k=0 or duplicates. Mutating a after build.

title: A range add is two point writes.
lede: To add x on [l,r] many times, do not loop the range. Write diff[l]+=x and diff[r+1]−=x. After all updates, a[i] = a[i-1] + diff[i] reconstructs the array in one pass. Each update O(1), build O(n).
diagram: 1 zeros n=5. add +2 on [1,3]: diff=[0,2,0,0,-2]. 2 add +1 on [0,4]: diff=[1,2,0,0,-2] and we needed diff[5] unused. 3 prefix: 1,3,3,3,1. Caption: corporate flight bookings, range addition, car pooling (capacity as a diff on trips).
what: Difference is the inverse of prefix. Point writes on the derivative, then integrate. 2D: four corners of a rectangle.
why: Many range updates, one final array. Car pooling: +passengers at start, − at end, scan to see if cap holds. Calendar busy times.
trap: Looping i=l..r anyway. r+1 off the array — allocate n+1. Mixing 0-based events with 1-based. Using this when you also need random range queries in between — then Fenwick.

title: Best ending here, or start over.
lede: Kadane: walk left to right. At i, the best subarray ending at i is either a[i] alone or a[i] glued to the best ending at i-1. cur = max(a[i], cur+a[i]); ans = max(ans, cur). One pass, O(n), O(1) extra. The empty subarray is a policy: usually not allowed if the problem wants at least one element.
diagram: Left (hit): [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]. cur/ans walk:  -2|-2; 1|1; -2|1; 4|4; 3|4; 5|5; 6|6; 1|6; 5|6. Window [4,-1,2,1]=6. Right: all negative. cur always a[i]; ans is the largest (least negative) element — do not reset to 0 unless empty is allowed.
what: Optimal substructure on 'best ending at i'. DP with two variables. Can recover the bounds by storing start when you reset.
why: Maximum subarray (LeetCode 53). Maximum circular (kadane + total−min-subarray). If they say contiguous, think Kadane before n².
trap: Initializing ans=0 so an all-negative array answers 0. Non-contiguous 'max subsequence' — that's a different problem (sum the positives). 2D max rectangle is Kadane on compressed rows, not one line.

title: Remember what you already saw.
lede: Two-sum: indices i < j with a[i]+a[j]=target. Nested loop is O(n²). Hash map: at i, if target−a[i] is in the map, return those indices; else map[a[i]]=i. One pass, average O(n). Sorted two-pointers is O(n) after sort but loses original indices unless you store them.
diagram: 1 a=[3,2,4] t=6. i=0 store 3→0. i=1 need 4, miss, store 2→1. i=2 need 2, hit 1 → [1,2]. 2 Same number twice: [3,3] t=6 — look up before insert. 3 Sorted variant: lo/hi, move the side that overshoots (plate 54).
what: Need indices → hash. Need any pair on sorted data → two pointers. Need all unique pairs → sort + two pointers + skip dups (then 3Sum).
why: The first LeetCode problem and the hashmap pattern that repeats in 3Sum family, two-sum in a BST, two-sum less than k.
trap: Using the same index twice (look up after insert, or target=2*a[i]). Sorting in place when the caller wanted original indices. Two pointers on unsorted data.

title: Sort. Then two pointers for three.
lede: 3Sum: unique triples a+b+c=0. Sort first. Fix i, then two-pointers on i+1..n-1 for the pair that sums to −a[i]. Skip duplicate a[i] and duplicate lo/hi values so each triple is unique. O(n²) time, O(1) extra besides sort.
diagram: Left (hit): [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4] sorted [-4,-1,-1,0,1,2]. i at -1 (first), lo/hi find [-1,0,1] and [-1,-1,2]. Skip the second -1 as a fix. Right: hashset of pairs per i also works but harder to unique; two pointers after sort is the expected write.
what: k-sum generalizes: sort, recurse k-1, two-pointers at k=2. Skip dups at every level. 4Sum is this with one more loop, still O(n³).
why: LeetCode 15/16/18. The pattern is 'reduce to 2Sum on a sorted array.' Say uniqueness is skip-dups, not an extra set of tuples (that is slower to write and hash).
trap: Not sorting. Not skipping dups — floods the answer with repeats. Moving both lo and hi, or neither, when the sum is wrong. Starting lo at 0 so a[i] can pair with itself on the left.

title: Prefix times suffix. Skip i.
lede: Product of the array except a[i], without division (zeroes would die, and the spec forbids it). left[i] = product of a[0..i). right[i] = product of a[i+1..]. answer[i] = left[i]*right[i]. Then drop the extra arrays: one output array as left, multiply a running suffix from the right.
diagram: a=[1,2,3,4]. left=[1,1,2,6]. right=[24,12,4,1]. ans=[24,12,8,6]. In-place: after left pass ans=[1,1,2,6]; suffix=1; i=3: ans[3]*=1 suffix=4; i=2 ans[2]*=4 suffix=12; i=1 ans[1]*=12 suffix=24; i=0 ans[0]*=24. Caption: O(n) time, O(1) extra besides output.
what: Prefix/suffix products. Zeros: at most one zero → that index gets the product of the rest, others 0. Two zeros → all 0.
why: LeetCode 238. A poster child for 'don't divide, precompute both sides.' Same shape as trapping rain two-pass max (plate 155).
trap: Division. Multiplying the whole array then dividing by a[i] (fails on 0, fails the spec). left[i] including a[i]. Using O(n) extra after they asked O(1) extra — mention the running suffix.

title: Three pointers. Three colors.
lede: Dutch national flag: partition an array of three values (0,1,2) in one pass. lo writes the next 0, hi writes the next 2, mid scans. Meet a 0: swap with lo++, mid++. Meet a 2: swap with hi--, do not mid++ (the new mid is unseen). Meet a 1: mid++.
diagram: Left (hit): [2,0,2,1,1,0]. Invariant: [0,lo) is 0s, [lo,mid) is 1s, (hi,n) is 2s, [mid,hi] unknown. Right: why not mid++ on a 2 — you just swapped in an unknown. Caption: also the 3-way partition inside quicksort for duplicates.
what: One pass, O(1) extra, not a counting sort (though counting also works for 3 values — they often forbid it or ask one-pass in-place).
why: LeetCode 75 Sort Colors. Interview tests in-place partition invariants. Same bones as quicksort's pivot split (plate 163).
trap: mid++ after swapping a 2. Using a sort. Counting sort when they said 'one pass, constant space' — counting is valid; say it, then write the three-pointer if they want the Dijkstra partition.

title: Reverse all. Reverse the parts.
lede: Rotate right by k: last k items move to the front. k %= n. Extra array is O(n) space. In-place: reverse the whole array, reverse [0,k), reverse [k,n). Each item walks to its final index. Cycle-swap (jump i → i+k) is the other O(1) write — gcd cycles.
diagram: 1 [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] k=3. 2 reverse all [7,6,5,4,3,2,1]. 3 reverse first 3 [5,6,7,4,3,2,1]. 4 reverse rest [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. Caption: left rotate by k is right rotate by n-k, or reverse in the other grouping.
what: Right rotate: a[i] ← a[(i−k) mod n]. Three reverses prove it: the block that should be first is reversed to the front, then unreversed.
why: LeetCode 189. Also: rotate a matrix 90° is a different plate (197). Tests modulo and in-place thinking.
trap: Forgetting k %= n (k=n should be identity; k>n otherwise index error). Reversing [0,k] inclusive wrong. Using extra memory after O(1) space was required. Rotating left vs right.

title: Fill from the back.
lede: Merge two sorted arrays. If nums1 has spare room at the end (length m+n), write from the back: the largest remaining goes to index m+n-1. Forward merge would overwrite unread nums1. If you own a new array, two pointers from the front are fine (merge lists, plate 146).
diagram: Left (hit): nums1=[1,4,7,0,0,0] m=3, nums2=[2,5,6] n=3. i=2,j=2,w=5. 7 vs 6 → write 7; 4 vs 6 → 6; 4 vs 5 → 5; rest 1,2,4. Right: if you start at 0, writing 1,2,… clobbers 4 and 7 still needed. Caption: leftover nums2 copies; leftover nums1 already in place.
what: O(m+n) time, O(1) extra when the tail is free. Same pattern: merge from the side that has spare slots.
why: LeetCode 88. Also the last step of merge sort. Interviews watch whether you clobber.
trap: Merging forward in nums1. Off-by-one on m+n-1. Copying nums1 leftovers unnecessarily. Sorted-descending arrays — then fill from the front.

title: A write head. A read head.
lede: Remove duplicates (or zeroes, or a value) in-place on a sorted array: one pointer writes the next kept slot, the other reads. Fast scans; slow only advances when you keep. Order of kept items stays. Return the new length; the tail is garbage.
diagram: 1 Sorted dups [0,0,1,1,1,2,2]. slow=0. fast=1..: write when a[fast]!=a[slow], slow++, assign. Result [0,1,2,…] len=3. 2 Move zeroes: write non-zeros forward, then fill the rest with 0. 3 Remove element val: write if a[fast]!=val. Caption: two pointers same direction (plate 54).
what: O(n) time, O(1) extra. Sorted is what makes 'equal to previous kept' the dup test. Unsorted dups need a set (extra space) or sort first.
why: LeetCode 26/27/283. The write/read split shows up in any compact-the-array problem.
trap: Deleting from a list while indexing forward (skip). Using extra array after in-place was required. For 'at most twice' (LC 80): compare with a[slow-2], not a[slow-1].

title: The deque front is the max.
lede: Sliding window maximum: for every window of k, the max. Heap of k is O(n log k) and stale indices need lazy skip. Better: a deque of indices, values decreasing. Incoming a[r]: pop back while smaller (they will never be max). Pop front if it left the window. Front is the answer.
diagram: Left (hit): a=[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7] k=3. Windows max 3,3,5,5,6,7. Deque after r=2: indices of 3,-1. r=4 (5): pop -1,3 both <5. Right: why decreasing — a smaller left of a larger dies; a larger left stays until it slides out. Caption: each index enter/leave once → O(n).
what: Monotonic deque (also window min, first negative in window). Store indices not values so you can expire r-k.
why: LeetCode 239. Hard-for-SDE1, expected-for-SDE2. Pattern: 'candidates in a queue, front is best, back is newest.'
trap: Storing values so you cannot tell expiry. Heap without checking index. Nested max() per window — O(nk). Popping the front when it is still inside the window.

title: Grow until a repeat. Then shrink.
lede: Longest substring without repeating characters: variable window (plate 55). Expand r. If s[r] is already in the window, advance l until it is not (jump using last-seen index). Track max length. O(n) with a map char → last index.
diagram: s=abcabcbb. r walks: a b c  — len 3; next a, move l past previous a; window bca len 3; then cab, abc, cb, b. ans=3. last={a:0,b:1,c:2} then a updates to 3, l=1. Caption: l = max(l, last[c]+1) so l never moves backward.
what: Need uniqueness in a contiguous slice → window + set or last-index map. Set version: while s[r] in set, remove s[l], l++.
why: LeetCode 3. The canonical variable-window. Same bones as longest with at most k distinct, replacement (plate 139).
trap: Restarting from r every time a duplicate appears — O(n²). Letting l move backward when last[c] is old (outside the window). Counting arrays vs characters (bytes vs Unicode).

title: Cover t. Then shrink. That's the window.
lede: Minimum window substring: smallest slice of s that covers every char of t (with counts). Expand r, increment have when a needed char's count is met. When have==need, shrink l as far as you can, record best, then break the cover and repeat. O(|s|+|t|).
diagram: Left (hit): s=ADOBECODEBANC t=ABC. First cover ADOBEC, shrink to BEC? no — CODEBA still missing? Walk to BANC, shrink to BANC length 4. Right: need map A1 B1 C1. have is how many of those requirements are currently satisfied, not the raw count of matching letters.
what: Two maps or a deficit counter. Window is valid iff every t-char is covered. Among valids, minimize r-l+1 (and often the leftmost).
why: LeetCode 76. Hard window. Same pattern: 'smallest window that satisfies a counter.' Also: find all anagrams (fixed need, window size |p|).
trap: Comparing full maps every step — slow to write, easy to get wrong; use have/need ints. Shrinking past a required char without decrementing have. Case sensitivity. t having duplicates and treating it as a set.

title: You may flip k. That's still a window.
lede: Longest repeating character replacement: you may change up to k letters. In a window, keep the count of the most frequent char. The rest of the window must be flipped: if window_len − maxf > k, shrink left. The window never needs to shrink more than one because we only care about the longest.
diagram: 1 s=AABABBA k=1. Window AABA — maxf=3, len=4, 4-3=1 ≤k. AABABB — 6-4=2>k, shrink. 2 Invariant: maxf is the best count seen in the current window. 3 You do not recompute maxf down when shrinking — it may be stale high, which only makes you stricter; still correct for the max length.
what: Valid window: at most k chars are not the mode. Fruit into baskets, at most k distinct, are cousins.
why: LeetCode 424. Teaches 'window cost = len − best.' Also 1004 max consecutive 1s with k flips (same, binary).
trap: Restarting DP O(n²). Forgetting k=0 is just longest run. Updating maxf on shrink (optional; if you do, it is also correct). Thinking you must pick the letter first — the mode of the window is the pick.

title: The first true. The last true.
lede: Binary search on a sorted array with duplicates: lower bound = first index where a[i] ≥ x (first true). Upper bound = first index where a[i] > x. Last occurrence is upper-1 if it equals x. The predicate must be monotonic: false,false,…,true,true.
diagram: Left (hit): a=[1,2,2,2,4] x=2. First: while lo<hi, mid=(lo+hi)//2; if a[mid]>=2: hi=mid else lo=mid+1 → 1. Last: if a[mid]<=2: lo=mid+1 else hi=mid → lo-1=3. Right: the bug mid=(lo+hi)//2 with hi=mid-1 vs hi=mid — pick a template and an invariant (plate 53).
what: Two searches, O(log n). Unsorted: cannot. Count of x = last-first+1, or 0 if missing.
why: LeetCode 34. Also: insert position, first bad version (first true), capacity-to-ship (plate 142) is the same 'first true' on a predicate.
trap: Returning any match (classic bisect) when they asked first/last. Infinite loop: lo=mid on a 2-length range without making progress. Checking a[mid]==x and scanning outward — that is O(n) on all-equal arrays.

title: One half is sorted. Search there.
lede: Rotated sorted array: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Still O(log n). At mid, at least one half is sorted (unless duplicates blur it). If the left half is sorted and the target sits in it, drop the right; else drop the left. Mirror for a sorted right half.
diagram: 1 lo=0 hi=6 mid=3 val=7. left 4..7 sorted. t=0 not in [4,7] → lo=mid+1. 2 now [0,1,2], ordinary binary. 3 Find min (pivot): if a[mid]>a[hi], min is to the right; else hi=mid. Caption: with duplicates (LC 81), when a[lo]==a[mid]==a[hi] you can only lo++ / hi-- — worst O(n).
what: Still a binary search with an extra sorted-half test. Finding the rotation index then ordinary search is two log n passes — also correct.
why: LeetCode 33/81/153. Interview favorite because the invariant is easy to get almost right.
trap: Assuming both halves sorted. Using a[0] as the split when there are duplicates. Off-by-one on inclusive ranges. Not handling already-sorted (rotation 0).

title: Binary search the answer, not the array.
lede: When the array is not sorted but the answer is monotonic — 'can we finish with capacity m?' is false for small m and true for large — binary search m. Check(m) is a linear scan. Time O(n log RANGE). Koko eating bananas, ship packages, split array largest sum, minimize max distance.
diagram: Left (hit): piles=[3,6,7,11] h=8. lo=1 hi=11. mid=6: hours=ceil 1+1+2+2=6 ≤8 → try smaller. Ans 4. Right: the predicate can(mid) must be monotonic. If it flickers, you cannot binary search it. Caption: lo is the first true. Initialize hi to max(piles) or sum, depending on the problem.
what: Search the solution space. You need a numeric range and a yes/no that flips once. Integer division / ceil: (x+m-1)//m.
why: SDE-2 screens love this. Once you say 'monotonic in the guess,' the rest is a first-true template (plate 140).
trap: Binary searching the index array which is unsorted. Off-by-one on lo=mid vs hi=mid. Integer overflow on hi=sum. check() using / instead of ceil.

title: A peak is bigger than both neighbors.
lede: A peak is an index with a[i] > neighbors (edges: one neighbor). Any array has a peak. Binary search: if a[mid] < a[mid+1], a peak sits to the right (the array is climbing). Else a peak sits at mid or left. O(log n). 2D peak: pick a mid column, find its max row, move toward the bigger neighbor column.
diagram: Left (hit): [1,3,2,1]. mid=1 val=3 > both → peak. [1,2,3,1]: mid=1 val=2<3 → go right. Right: bitonic (strict increase then decrease) — the peak is the unique max; same walk. Caption: this is not 'find 1 in a mountain then binary both sides' (LC 1095) — that's peak plus two searches.
what: Local maximum via a monotonic 'is the slope up?' test. Duplicates: problem usually promises a[i] != a[i+1].
why: LeetCode 162/852. Interview: they want log n, not a linear scan. Teaches binary search without a target.
trap: Comparing to both neighbors every step and shrinking wrong. Infinite loop on mid. Assuming the global max is required — any peak is enough unless they said mountain array peak (unique).

title: If they meet, there is a cycle.
lede: Cycle detection without extra memory: slow walks one, fast walks two. If there is a cycle, fast laps slow and they meet. If fast hits null, no cycle. Meeting does not give the start — that's plate 147. A set of seen nodes is O(n) space and also correct; they often want O(1) space.
diagram: 1 1→2→3→4→5→3. slow/fast start at 1. 2 after steps: meet at 4 or 5 depending on start. 3 no cycle: fast becomes null. Caption: check fast and fast.next before fast.next.next. Same idea finds the midpoint (fast hits end, slow is mid).
what: Floyd. Time O(n), space O(1). Proof sketch: relative speed 1, they close the cycle length.
why: LeetCode 141. Also: happy number (cycle in a function), find duplicate number (cycle in a functional graph of indices).
trap: fast = fast.next.next without a null guard. Starting slow at head and fast at head.next inconsistently vs both at head — both work if the loop test matches. Using a set after they asked O(1) space.

title: Three pointers reverse a list.
lede: Reverse a singly linked list in O(n)/O(1): prev=null, cur=head. nxt=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=nxt. Return prev. Recursion (reverse the tail, then head.next.next=head) is O(n) stack — fine for small n, not for 10^5.
diagram: Left (hit): 1→2→3→null. snapshots: null←1 2→3; null←1←2 3; null←1←2←3. Right: reverse a sublist [l,r] — dummy, walk to l-1, reverse r-l+1 links, reconnect. Caption: reverse k-group is this in chunks (LC 25).
what: Iterative three pointers. Dummy for sublist reverse so the predecessor is easy. Doubly-linked reverse is swap prev/next everywhere.
why: LeetCode 206/92/25. Palindrome list: reverse the second half (plate 149). Always draw one node flipping.
trap: Losing nxt. Returning head (now the tail). Recursing the whole list in production. Off-by-one when reversing a range (1-indexed l,r).

title: Dummy head. Pick the smaller.
lede: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list. Dummy sentinel, tail walks. Each step: attach the smaller head, advance that list. Then attach whatever remains. O(m+n), O(1) extra. Do not allocate new nodes unless asked — relink.
diagram: 1 dummy. 1→4→5 and 1→2→3→6. 2 pick 1 (a), 1 (b), 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. 3 return dummy.next. Caption: merge k lists is this in a heap (plate 161) or pairwise.
what: Same as merging arrays from the front (you own new links, no clobber). Recursion: return the smaller node, its next = merge(rest) — O(n) stack.
why: LeetCode 21. Foundation for merge sort on lists (LC 148) and k-way merge.
trap: Forgetting the leftover tail. Using a dummy and returning dummy not dummy.next. Comparing node vs node.val. Creating new nodes when relink was enough.

title: Meet, then walk from head.
lede: Where the cycle begins: first find a meeting point (plate 144). Then put one pointer at head, keep the other at the meeting point, walk both by one. They meet at the entrance. Why: if head-to-start is a, start-to-meet is b, cycle is c, then a = k c − b — the remaining walk around equals a.
diagram: 1 1→2→3→4→5→3. Meet say at 5. 2 p=head (1), q=5. Step: 2 and 3, then 3 and 4, then 4 and 5, then 5 and 3, then 3 and 3. Start=3. 3 No extra memory. Caption: find duplicate number (LC 287) is this on nums[i] as next.
what: Two-phase Floyd. Phase 1 detects; phase 2 locates. If you only needed yes/no, stop at phase 1.
why: LeetCode 142. Also: duplicate in 1..n array as a linked list of indices. Interviewers want the second phase, not just 'I would store nodes in a set.'
trap: Resetting both to head. Walking fast at speed 2 in phase 2. Off-by-one proofs you don't need to recite — state a = remaining in the cycle. Mutating next to detect (ruins the list).

title: Same leftover length. Then they meet.
lede: Intersection of two singly lists: they share a suffix (by pointer, not value). Lengths may differ. Trick: pointer A walks list A then B; pointer B walks B then A. The second half of both walks is the same length, so they hit the join together — or both hit null.
diagram: Left (hit): A = 1-2-3-4-5, B = 9-4-5, join at 4. A walks 5+2, B walks 2+5, meet at 4. Right: no join — both finish at null after n+m. Caption: counting lengths and skipping the prefix is the same idea, two passes explicit.
what: O(n+m) time, O(1) space. Equality is node identity, not val==val (two 4s might be different nodes).
why: LeetCode 160. Tests pointer fluency without extra sets. Contrast: if values matter, it's a different problem.
trap: Comparing values. Putting all of A in a set (works, uses O(n)). Cutting the lists. Off-by-one when skipping length diff: skip |nA-nB| on the longer, then walk together.

title: Split. Reverse the back. Weave.
lede: Reorder list to L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1…. Three algorithms you already have: slow/fast finds the mid and cuts. Reverse the second half (plate 145). Merge by weaving (one from each). Palindrome list is split + reverse + compare instead of weave.
diagram: 1 1-2-3-4-5. slow at 3, cut 3.next=null. second=4-5 → reverse 5-4. 2 weave 1-2-3 and 5-4 → 1-5-2-4-3. 3 palindrome: compare 1-2-3 vs reversed second. Caption: even/odd length: for odd, the mid stays in the first half.
what: Compose primitives. O(n) time, O(1) space. Do not use an array of nodes unless they allow O(n) space.
why: LeetCode 143 / 234. Interview: can you sequence three known tricks without mixing the pointers.
trap: Not cutting the first half — a cycle. Reversing including the mid on odd lists so the mid points at itself. Weaving without a temp for next.

title: Hash finds. The list splices.
lede: LRU cache: get and put in O(1), evict the least recently used when over capacity. Hash map key → node for O(1) find. Doubly-linked list (dummy head/tail) for O(1) move-to-front and evict-from-back (plate 104). Recency is the list order; the map is only an index.
diagram: Left (hit): cap=2. put 1, put 2, get 1 (move 1 to tail), put 3 (evict 2). list dummyH-2-1-dummyT then 1 moves, then 2 unlinked 3 added. Right: why not a queue + map only: queue cannot unlink a middle key in O(1). Caption: LFU needs a second structure (freq lists).
what: get: map lookup, move node to most-recent, return val or -1. put: update+move, or insert; if over cap, unlink the least-recent and delete from map.
why: LeetCode 146. The design question. Say both structures in the first sentence. Then dummy sentinels so you never null-check head/tail.
trap: Python OrderedDict is the language gift — know it, still be able to draw the DLL. Evicting the most recent. Forgetting to update the map on eviction. Singly-linked list scans.
